extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science; philosophers of science; researchers learning principles of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging and using scientific hypotheses and experiments: when to accept/reject hypotheses, what counts as decisive (experimentum crucis), the roles of descriptive/representative hypotheses, and the classification of empirical vs theoretical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: No clear and absolute conflict with known laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Provided that there be no clear and absolute conflict with known laws of nature, there is no hypothesis so improbable or apparently inconceivable that it may not be rendered probable, or even approximately certain, by a sufficient number of concordances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficulties of conception are not alone sufficient grounds to reject a hypothesis; only when a hypothesis breaks distinctly the primary laws of thought and nature should it be rejected. (Examples discussed: undulatory ether hypotheses and gravity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement with particular facts; single absolute conflict is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: Before we accept a new hypothesis it must be shown to agree not only with the previously known laws of nature, but also with the particular facts which it is framed to explain. A single absolute conflict between fact and hypothesis is fatal to the hypothesis; falsa in una, falsa in omnibus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothesis must agree with all established facts it aims to explain. Occasional misinterpretation of a fact or error in an assumed law may sometimes be considered, but a genuine absolute contradiction overturns a theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis should enable deductive anticipation of new facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A good hypothesis, besides agreeing with facts already noticed, will furnish us with distinct credentials by enabling us to anticipate deductively series of facts which are not already connected and accounted for by any equally probable hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothesis gains credibility if it predicts previously unobserved phenomena that are later verified; such foreknowledge is strong evidence in its favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and value of accordances determine probability; no finite number yields certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot lay down any precise rule as to the number of accordances which can establish the truth of an hypothesis... While, on the one hand, no finite number of accordances will give entire certainty, the probability of the hypothesis will increase very rapidly with the number of accordances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the quantity and quality (value) of confirming instances; probability increases with concordant evidence but absolute certainty by induction is unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentum crucis must decide between rival theories (negative and positive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any experiment which decides between two rival theories may be called an Experimentum Crucis... A crucial experiment must not simply confirm one theory, but must negative another; it must decide a mind which is in equilibrium, as Bacon says, between two equally plausible views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To count as crucial the experiment must (a) produce results agreeing with one hypothesis but not the other, (b) be performed when rival theories are comparably plausible, and (c) thereby settle the choice. Examples: the velocity-of-light measurements distinguishing corpuscular and undulatory theories; Copernican predictions of planetary phases; Pascal's barometer experiment as illustrative but not always strictly 'crucial' unless it negatives a rival theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reject a hypothesis solely for being hard to conceive
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere difficulties of conception must not discredit a theory which otherwise agrees with facts, and we must only reject hypotheses which are inconceivable in the sense of breaking distinctly the primary laws of thought and nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical or intuitive awkwardness (e.g., action at a distance for gravity) is not a sufficient reason for rejection if empirical agreement is strong; focus on empirical conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must allow precise calculation or rigorous verification where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure [of a theory] was in the first and third requisites; for, as already remarked, the theory did not allow of precise calculation of planetary motions, and was thus incapable of rigorous verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A viable physical theory should enable precise predictions or computations that can be tested; theories that cannot be subjected to rigorous verification are weak (example: Cartesian vortices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive hypotheses are mere names and not explanatory
rubrics_metrics.description: There are hypotheses which we may call descriptive hypotheses, and which serve for little else than to furnish convenient names... if these theories be understood as more than convenient modes of describing the phenomena, they are altogether invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive hypotheses (mere labels or analogies) add nothing to explanation and are unsatisfactory if treated as true mechanisms; they typically fail to suggest new experiments (example: classical 'electric fluid', Newton's 'fits'). Treat them as provisional labels only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative hypotheses permissible if they embody real analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardly to be distinguished from descriptive hypotheses are certain imaginary objects which we frame for the ready comprehension of a subject... Such devices may be called Representative Hypotheses, and they are only permissible so far as they embody analogies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mental models (e.g., pendulum for undulation, ballot-box for probability) to aid thought, but ensure they rest on genuine analogies and do not mislead about underlying mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce new agents only when required; avoid mixing discrete things
rubrics_metrics.description: We are at freedom to imagine the existence of a new agent... so long as there are phenomena incapable of explanation from known causes. But such hypotheses will do much harm whenever they divert us from attempts to reconcile the facts with known laws, or when they lead us to mix up discrete things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postulate new entities (vital force, resisting medium, protoplasm) only provisionally and with caution; ensure they do not prevent attempts to reconcile phenomena with established laws or obscure distinctions between different things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify knowledge: empirical, explained, predicted, theory-only
rubrics_metrics.description: We may be acquainted with facts which have not yet been brought into accordance with any hypothesis (empirical); facts first observed empirically then brought into accordance by hypothesis (explained); facts anticipated by theory and afterwards verified by experiment (predicted); knowledge accepted solely on the ground of theory and incapable of experimental confirmation with current instruments (theory-only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating scientific claims, note which class they belong to—empirical facts, explained/generalised facts, theory-predicted facts, or theory-only claims—and weigh their epistemic value accordingly; sciences typically progress from empirical to explained to predictive knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical knowledge: facts unconnected to hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: By empirical knowledge we mean such as is derived directly from the examination of detached facts, and rests entirely on those facts, without corroboration from other branches of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize many branches of science remain largely empirical (collections of disconnected facts). Empirical observations (e.g., rainbow conditions, refractive powers correlated with combustibility in Newton's observations) can later become theoretical but initially should be treated as data requiring explanation.
